chem_ocrb.2.6.summary: This topic covers the foundational principles of covalent bonding, where non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons to achieve a stable noble gas electronic configuration. Students must master drawing dot and cross diagrams for simple molecules and giant covalent structures, deriving empirical formulae from molecular formulae or analytical data, and interpreting various 2D and 3D molecular representations. Achieving a grade 9 requires rigorous precision in describing electrostatic attractions between shared electron pairs and positive nuclei, alongside clear identification of molecular structures and limitations of chemical models.

core.p: Covalent bonding occurs strictly between non-metal atoms. Because non-metals have relatively high electronegativities and lack enough valence electrons to easily lose them, they achieve stability by sharing pairs of electrons.
bullets: Formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei of the bonded atoms.
Each atom typically shares enough electrons to attain a full outer shell, mimicking the nearest noble gas structure (the octet rule, or duplet for hydrogen).
Can involve single covalent bonds (one shared pair), double covalent bonds (two shared pairs), or triple covalent bonds (three shared pairs).
Results in the formation of discrete molecules or giant covalent lattices.

callouts.p: A chemical bond formed when two non-metal atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
Never state that covalent bonding involves the transfer of electrons or the attraction between oppositely charged ions; that is ionic bonding.

fig.cap: Figure 1: Formation of a single covalent bond in a hydrogen molecule (H2) via the sharing of two electrons.

core.h: Dot and Cross Diagrams for Simple Molecules
core.p: Dot and cross diagrams model how outer shell electrons are shared in covalent compounds. By convention, electrons from one atom are shown as dots and electrons from the other as crosses.
bullets: Only the outer shell electrons need to be drawn for complex atoms, though inner shells can be included if explicitly requested.
Hydrogen chloride (HCl): chlorine shares one electron with hydrogen, giving hydrogen 2 and chlorine 8 outer electrons.
Water (H2O): oxygen shares one electron with each of the two hydrogen atoms, leaving two lone pairs on the oxygen atom.
Carbon dioxide (CO2): carbon shares two electrons with each oxygen atom, forming a double covalent bond with each oxygen.
Ammonia (NH3) and Methane (CH4): nitrogen shares three and carbon shares four electrons with hydrogen atoms respectively.

callouts.p: Always check your final diagram: every H must touch 2 electrons, and period 2 elements (C, N, O, F) must be surrounded by 8 electrons in total.

core.p: Chemists use various models to represent molecules, each with specific advantages and limitations regarding what they show about bonding, structure, and 3D shape.
bullets: Displayed formulae: use solid lines to represent single covalent bonds. Easy to draw and show connectivity, but do not show 3D shape or electron distribution accurately.
3D ball-and-stick models: use spheres for atoms and sticks for bonds. Useful for visualising three-dimensional spatial arrangement, but bonds are rigid and atoms are disproportionately small.
Space-filling models: show the relative sizes of atoms and how they pack together in 3D space, but obscure internal bond angles and connectivity.
Dot and cross diagrams: excellent for showing electron origin and outer shell configurations, but static and do not represent physical bond angles.

head: Model Type
Main Advantage
Main Disadvantage
rows: Clear representation of connectivity and bonds
Fails to show 3D shape and bond angles
Does not represent true atomic scale or electron cloud
Accurate relative atomic size and crowding
Difficult to see back atoms and precise bond paths

callouts.p: No single model is perfect. Examiners frequently ask you to state why a ball-and-stick or dot-and-cross model has limitations (e.g., they do not show continuous movement or true 3D electron cloud densities).

core.p: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element present in a compound. It can be calculated from mass data or percentage composition by mass.
bullets: Step 1: Write down the masses or percentages of each element given in the question.
Step 2: Divide each mass/percentage by the relative atomic mass (Ar) of that element to find the number of moles.
Step 3: Divide all the resulting mole values by the smallest number of moles calculated.
Step 4: If the numbers are not whole numbers, multiply all by a common factor (e.g., 1.5 x 2 = 3, 1.33 x 3 = 4) to obtain the simplest whole-number ratio.

callouts.p: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
Never round numbers like 1.99 or 2.01 until the very final step. 1.99 rounds to 2, but 1.5 must be multiplied by 2 to become 3.

core.h: Deriving Empirical Formula from Molecular Formula
core.p: For simple molecular compounds, the molecular formula shows the exact number of atoms of each element in a molecule, whereas the empirical formula is its reduced ratio.
bullets: If a molecular formula is C4H10, find the highest common factor of the subscripts (which is 2).
Divide each subscript by 2 to get the empirical formula: C2H5.
If a molecular formula is C6H12O6, divide by the common factor 6 to get the empirical formula CH2O.
For water (H2O), the molecular and empirical formulae are identical because the ratio 2:1 cannot be simplified further.

callouts.p: Ionic compounds always use empirical formulae because giant lattices do not consist of discrete molecules. Covalent substances can have molecular formulae that are multiples of their empirical formulae.

core.p: Substances consisting of simple molecules have distinct physical properties governed by the strength of their internal covalent bonds versus their weak intermolecular forces.
bullets: Low melting and boiling points: little thermal energy is required to overcome the weak intermolecular forces between molecules, not the strong covalent bonds.
Do not conduct electricity: molecules are electrically neutral overall and contain no overall free-moving charged particles (ions or delocalised electrons).
Most are gases, liquids, or low-melting-point solids at room temperature and pressure.
Solubility: many are insoluble in water unless they can hydrogen bond or react with it, though non-polar molecules dissolve well in non-polar organic solvents.

callouts.p: When a molecular substance melts or boils, you break the weak intermolecular forces between molecules, NOT the strong covalent bonds holding the atoms together inside the molecule.

core.p: Unlike simple molecules, giant covalent structures (macromolecules) consist of a massive network of atoms linked by strong covalent bonds extending throughout the entire structure.
bullets: Diamond, graphite, and silicon dioxide (silica) are classic examples of giant covalent structures.
Very high melting and boiling points: a vast amount of thermal energy is required to break millions of strong covalent bonds.
Insoluble in water and organic solvents because covalent bonds within the lattice are far too strong to be disrupted by solvent interactions.
Except for graphite and graphene, they do not conduct electricity because all outer electrons are tied up in localized covalent bonds with no free charge carriers.

callouts.p: Giant covalent = extremely high melting point and hard (except graphite, which is soft due to weak inter-layer forces).

fig.cap: Figure 3: Tetrahedral structure of diamond, showing each carbon bonded to four others with strong covalent bonds.

core.h: Allotropes of Carbon: Diamond and Graphite
core.p: Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state. Carbon exhibits several remarkable allotropes due to its unique bonding versatility.
bullets: Diamond: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement. Extremely hard with a very high melting point (~3550 °C).

Graphite: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms, forming hexagonal layers. Layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces, allowing them to slide past each other (making graphite soft and slippery).
Graphite electrical conductivity: each carbon atom has one unbonded outer electron which becomes delocalised throughout the layers, allowing graphite to conduct electricity and heat.
Graphene: a single, one-atom-thick layer of graphite with exceptional strength and electrical conductivity.

callouts.p: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.

core.p: Fullerene molecules are hollow cages of carbon atoms, and carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with fascinating structural and electronic properties.
bullets: Buckminsterfullerene (C60): consists of 60 carbon atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons, forming a spherical football-like cage structure.
Carbon nanotubes: cylindrical fullerenes with high length-to-diameter ratios. They have very high tensile strength (resistance to breaking when pulled) and conduct electricity.
Applications: drug delivery systems in medicine, reinforcing materials in sports equipment (tennis rackets), and electronics.
Nanoparticles of carbon have huge surface area to volume ratios, making them extremely effective catalysts.

callouts.p: When explaining nanotube strength, mention that strong covalent bonds along the axis make them exceptionally difficult to break.

core.p: Polymers are very large molecules made by bonding many small monomer units together through covalent bonds in long chains.
bullets: Monomers are small, usually alkene-based molecules with a double covalent bond that can open up during polymerisation.
Poly(ethene) is formed when thousands of ethene molecules join end-to-end.
Represented by repeating units enclosed in brackets with a subscript 'n', e.g., [-CH2-CH2-]n.
Intermolecular forces between large polymer chains are stronger than those in small molecules, meaning polymers are solid at room temperature.

callouts.p: A large molecule formed by joining many small molecules (monomers) together through covalent bonds.

analogy.p: Imagine two students (non-metal atoms) who each need a specific textbook to finish their homework. Instead of buying separate books, they share a single copy kept in the middle of their desk so both can read it at the same time—this shared resource represents a covalent bond. The analogy breaks down because atoms share identical electron pairs symmetrically and electrostatic forces hold them together, whereas student sharing involves mutual agreement and social rules.

terms.d: A chemical bond formed by the sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
The actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
A particle consisting of two or more atoms chemically bound together by covalent bonds.
A lattice of atoms connected by a continuous network of strong covalent bonds.
Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state.
A molecule of carbon atoms in the form of a hollow sphere, ellipse, or tube.
A large chain-like molecule made from many repeating smaller units called monomers.
A small molecule that can join with other identical molecules to form a polymer.
Weak forces of attraction existing between discrete molecules.
An electron that is no longer bound to a single atom and is free to move throughout a structure.
A pair of outer shell electrons that is not shared between atoms.

mistakes.w: Melting covalent substances breaks covalent bonds.
mistakes.r: Melting simple molecular substances overcomes weak intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.

mistakes.w: Covalent bonds form between metals and non-metals.
mistakes.r: Covalent bonds form exclusively between non-metal atoms; metal-non-metal bonding is ionic.

mistakes.w: Empirical formula and molecular formula are always the same.
mistakes.r: Empirical is the simplest ratio; molecular is the actual number of atoms. They can be different (e.g., C2H4 vs CH2).

mistakes.w: Graphite conducts electricity because its layers slide.
mistakes.r: Graphite conducts electricity because of delocalised electrons between layers; sliding explains its softness, not conductivity.

mistakes.w: Simple molecules conduct electricity when melted.
mistakes.r: Simple molecules do not conduct electricity in any state because they have no overall charge or free ions/electrons.

mistakes.w: Diamond has free electrons and conducts electricity.
mistakes.r: Diamond has all four outer electrons locked in covalent bonds, so it has no free electrons and does not conduct.

mistakes.w: Dot and cross diagrams show exact 3D molecular geometry.
mistakes.r: Dot and cross diagrams only show electron sharing, not physical 3D shapes or bond angles.

exam.q: Explain why water has a low boiling point. (2 marks)
model: It has weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
Very little thermal energy is required to overcome these forces.
exam.tip: Never state that covalent bonds break when water boils.

exam.q: Draw a dot and cross diagram for a molecule of ammonia (NH3). Show outer shell electrons only. (3 marks)
model: Nitrogen drawn with 5 outer electrons and 3 hydrogen atoms each with 1 electron.
Three shared pairs of electrons between nitrogen and each hydrogen.
One unshared lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom.
exam.tip: Double-check that nitrogen is surrounded by 8 electrons and each hydrogen by 2.

exam.q: A compound contains 80% carbon and 20% hydrogen by mass. Calculate its empirical formula. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1). (4 marks)
model: Moles of C = 80 / 12 = 6.67
Moles of H = 20 / 1 = 20
Divide by smallest (6.67) to get ratio 1 : 3, so empirical formula is CH3.
exam.tip: Always layout your calculation in clear steps: Mass -> Moles -> Divide by smallest -> Ratio.

exam.q: Explain why graphite can conduct electricity but diamond cannot, despite both being made of carbon. (4 marks)
model: In graphite, each carbon is bonded to three other carbons, leaving one electron per atom delocalised.
These delocalised electrons are free to move throughout the structure and carry charge.
In diamond, each carbon is bonded to four other carbons in a tetrahedral network.
All outer electrons are locked in covalent bonds with no free charge carriers.
exam.tip: Comparison questions require you to write about BOTH substances explicitly.

exam.q: State the limitation of using a ball-and-stick model to represent a simple molecule. (1 mark)
model: Sticks are not real bonds and atoms are spaced out unnaturally / does not show true electron cloud density.
exam.tip: Keep answers concise and directly tied to model limitations.

exam.q: Derive the empirical formula of glucose, C6H12O6. (1 mark)
model: CH2O
exam.tip: Divide all subscripts by the highest common factor, which is 6.

exam.q: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point. (2 marks)
model: It is a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds.
A large amount of thermal energy is required to break these bonds.
exam.tip: Mention both giant covalent network and strong covalent bonds.

exam.q: Describe the structure and bonding in buckminsterfullerene (C60). (2 marks)
model: It consists of carbon atoms arranged in hollow spheres of pentagons and hexagons.
Atoms are covalently bonded within the molecule with weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
exam.tip: Distinguish between internal covalent bonds and intermolecular forces between fullerene spheres.

worked.q: Calculate the empirical formula of an oxide of phosphorus formed when 6.2 g of phosphorus reacts with oxygen to produce 14.2 g of phosphorus oxide. (Ar: P = 31, O = 16)
steps: Find mass of oxygen: 14.2 g total - 6.2 g phosphorus = 8.0 g oxygen.
Multiply by 2 to get whole numbers: P = 2, O = 5.

worked.q: A hydrocarbon has a molecular formula of C8H18. Determine its empirical formula.
steps: Find the highest common factor for 8 and 18, which is 2.
Divide each subscript by 2: Carbon = 8 / 2 = 4; Hydrogen = 18 / 2 = 9.

chem_ocrb.2.8.summary: This section covers organic chemistry and homologous series specifically for triple chemistry students under OCR GCSE Chemistry B. It explores the structures, functional groups, and chemical reactions of alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, and carboxylic acids. Mastering these families, their general formulae, and specific reactions allows you to predict chemical behaviour and write balanced equations for combustion, addition, esterification, and neutralisation.

core.h: Introduction to Homologous Series and Functional Groups
core.p: Organic compounds are organised into homologous series, which are families of molecules with the same general formula and similar chemical properties. Understanding these structural families is fundamental to organic chemistry.
bullets: A homologous series shares the same **functional group**, which determines its chemical reactions.
Successive members differ by a **-CH2-** unit in their molecular formulae.
As chain length increases, physical properties such as **boiling point** and viscosity increase due to stronger intermolecular forces.
They show a gradual change (trend) in physical properties down the series.

callouts.p: A family of compounds with the same general formula, similar chemical properties, and successive members differing by a -CH2- unit.

core.p: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms. They are relatively unreactive except when they burn or react with halogens under UV light.
bullets: General formula is **CnH2n+2**.
Described as **saturated** because they contain only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Undergo **complete combustion** in excess oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water.
Undergo **incomplete combustion** in limited oxygen, producing toxic carbon monoxide or carbon soot.
React with halogens (e.g., bromine) only in the presence of **ultraviolet light** through substitution reactions.

callouts.p: Alkanes react with halogens in UV light where a hydrogen atom is replaced by a halogen atom.

fig.cap: Comparison of structural representations of methane and ethane showing single covalent bonds.

core.p: Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond, making them unsaturated. This functional group makes them much more chemically reactive than alkanes.
bullets: General formula is **CnH2n** (for hydrocarbons with one double bond).
Described as **unsaturated** because they contain a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C).
Distinguished from alkanes using **bromine water**: alkenes turn orange-brown bromine water **colourless**.
Undergo **addition reactions** where the double bond opens up to bond with other atoms.
React with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form alkanes (hydrogenation).

callouts.p: Contains at least one carbon-carbon double covalent bond (C=C).
Always state that bromine water turns from orange-brown to colourless. Never write 'clear' (clear means transparent, like water).

core.p: Because of the reactive C=C double bond, alkenes undergo addition reactions with various reagents, breaking the pi bond and adding atoms across the carbon atoms.
bullets: **Reaction with hydrogen**: Ethene + Hydrogen -> Ethane (requires 150 °C and a **nickel catalyst**).
**Reaction with steam**: Ethene + Steam -> Ethanol (requires high temperature, pressure, and a **phosphoric acid catalyst**).
**Reaction with halogens**: Ethene + Bromine -> 1,2-dibromoethane (occurs rapidly at room temperature without UV light).
Addition reactions result in a single product molecule, meaning a **100% atom economy**.

callouts.p: Industrial method to manufacture ethanol using steam and a phosphoric acid catalyst.

fig.cap: Addition reaction of ethene with bromine showing the double bond opening up.

core.p: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl functional group (-OH). They are widely used as solvents, fuels, and in alcoholic drinks.
bullets: General formula is **CnH2n+1OH**.
Functional group is the **-OH** (hydroxyl) group.
Dissolve in water to form neutral solutions (pH 7).
React with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas and a metal alkoxide.
Undergo complete combustion to form carbon dioxide and water.
Can be oxidised (using acidified potassium dichromate) to form **carboxylic acids**.

callouts.p: Ethanol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to form ethanoic acid and water upon heating.

core.p: Ethanol can be produced industrially by fermenting sugars using yeast. This is a batch process using renewable resources.
bullets: Raw material is glucose (derived from plant material/sugars).
Uses enzymes in **yeast** as a biological catalyst.
Optimum temperature is around **37 °C**.
Must be carried out under **anaerobic conditions** (no oxygen) to prevent ethanol from oxidizing into ethanoic acid.
Word equation: Glucose -> Ethanol + Carbon dioxide.
Dilute ethanol solution is produced (approx 15% concentration before fractional distillation).

callouts.p: If the temperature is too high (>40 °C), yeast enzymes denature. If too low, the reaction rate is too slow.

core.p: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl functional group (-COOH). They behave as weak acids in aqueous solutions.
bullets: General formula is **CnH2n+1COOH**.
Functional group is the **-COOH** (carboxyl) group.
React with carbonates to produce a salt, water, and **carbon dioxide gas** (effervescence).
React with metals and alkalis just like typical mineral acids.
Described as **weak acids** because they only partially ionise in aqueous solution, resulting in a higher pH than strong acids of the same concentration.

callouts.p: An acid that is only partially ionized in aqueous solution.

core.p: It is vital to distinguish between concentration (amount of substance per volume) and strength (degree of ionisation).
bullets: **Strong acids** (like HCl, HNO3) are completely ionised in water.
**Weak acids** (like ethanoic acid) are only partially ionised, meaning an equilibrium is set up.
At the same concentration, weak acids have a higher pH than strong acids because they have a lower concentration of hydrogen ions (H+).
Because ionisation is reversible, reactions of weak acids can be slower than strong acids.

callouts.p: Concentrated/dilute refers to moles per dm3. Strong/weak refers to degree of ionisation.

core.p: Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters, which have characteristic sweet, fruity smells.
bullets: General reaction: Carboxylic acid + Alcohol -> **Ester + Water**.
Requires a concentrated **sulfuric acid catalyst** and heating under reflux.
Functional group in esters is the **-COO-** ester link.
Example: Ethanoic acid + Ethanol -> Ethyl ethanoate + Water.
Esters are volatile compounds used in perfumes, flavourings, and solvents.

callouts.p: The first part comes from the alcohol (changing -anol to -yl) and the second part from the acid (changing -anoic acid to -anoate).

core.p: Alkenes can act as monomers to form large chain molecules called polymers through addition polymerisation.
bullets: **Monomers** are small alkene molecules with a C=C double bond.
During polymerisation, the C=C double bonds open up and link together to form a long saturated chain (**polymer**).
The name of the polymer is poly(name of monomer), e.g., **poly(ethene)**.
The repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer, but with single bonds and extension bonds outside brackets.
Addition polymers are generally non-biodegradable, causing environmental disposal issues.

callouts.p: The process of joining many small monomer molecules together to form a long chain polymer.

analogy.p: Think of monomers as individual train carriages with special hitching hooks (double bonds). In an addition reaction or polymerisation, the hooks open up and link carriages together into a long train (the polymer). Where it breaks down: real molecules involve electron sharing and orbital overlap rather than mechanical hooks.

terms.d: A family of organic compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties.
An atom or group of atoms responsible for the typical chemical reactions of a molecule.
A compound containing only hydrogen and carbon with single covalent bonds only.
A hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon double covalent bond.
A reaction where two or more molecules react together to form a single product.
The breakdown of sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide using yeast enzymes anaerobically.
An organic compound containing the -COOH functional group that acts as a weak acid.
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.
An organic compound formed from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, containing the -COO- group.
A small molecule that can join with other molecules to form a polymer.
A large molecule formed by joining many repeating monomer units.
The addition of water or steam across the double bond of an alkene.

mistakes.w: Saying bromine water turns clear with alkenes.
mistakes.r: Bromine water turns from orange-brown to colourless.

mistakes.w: Confusing strength and concentration of acids.
mistakes.r: Strength refers to degree of ionisation; concentration refers to moles per dm3.

mistakes.w: Drawing polymers with double bonds in the repeating unit.
mistakes.r: Addition polymers have single bonds only in the main chain.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the catalyst for hydration of ethene.
Writing fermentation in the presence of air.
mistakes.r: Must be anaerobic to prevent oxidation to ethanoic acid.
Alkanes undergo substitution reactions in UV light; alkenes undergo addition.

exam.q: State the general formula for the homologous series of alkanes.
model: CnH2n+2

exam.q: Describe what is observed when ethene gas is bubbled through orange-brown bromine water.
model: Bromine water turns
from orange-brown to colourless

exam.q: Explain why carboxylic acids are described as weak acids compared to hydrochloric acid.
model: Carboxylic acids only partially ionise in aqueous solution
whereas hydrochloric acid is fully ionised
resulting in a higher pH for carboxylic acid at the same concentration

exam.q: Name the catalyst and conditions used in the industrial hydration of ethene to produce ethanol.
model: Phosphoric acid catalyst
High temperature
High pressure
exam.tip: Learn specific catalysts for each organic reaction.

exam.q: Write the word equation for the reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol.
model: Ethanoic acid + Ethanol ->
Ethyl ethanoate + Water
exam.tip: Remember water is the second product in esterification.

exam.q: Explain the conditions necessary for manufacturing ethanol by fermentation.
model: Yeast used as biological catalyst
Optimum temperature around 37 °C to maintain enzyme activity
Anaerobic conditions (no oxygen)
Prevents oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid
exam.tip: Include why anaerobic conditions are needed.

exam.q: Draw the repeating unit of poly(ethene).
model: Correct two carbon atoms with single bond and single H atoms attached
Square brackets with extension bonds passing through the brackets
exam.tip: Do not leave free radicals without bonds extending outside brackets.

exam.q: Explain why alkanes are described as saturated hydrocarbons.
model: Contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms (hydrocarbon)
Contains only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms (saturated)
exam.tip: Break down both parts of the term.

exam.q: Describe the reaction of propane with bromine in the presence of UV light.
model: Substitution reaction occurs
A hydrogen atom is replaced by a bromine atom
exam.tip: UV light is the key trigger for alkane halogenation.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of ethanol produced from 180 g of glucose during fermentation, assuming a 90% yield. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
steps: Theoretical mass of ethanol = 2 mol * 46 g/mol = 92 g

worked.q: Name the ester formed from methanol and propanoic acid, and give its molecular formula.
steps: Alcohol is methanol -> alkyl group is methyl
Acid is propanoic acid -> carboxylate group is propanoate
Propanoic acid part has 3 carbons (C2H5COO-), methanol part has 1 carbon (-CH3)
